name: FLORES-101
description: FLORES-101 is an evaluation benchmark consisting of 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia and professionally translated into 101 languages. The sentences cover a variety of topics and domains, sourced from Wikinews, Wikijunior, and WikiVoyage. The dataset enables evaluation of many-to-many multilingual translation systems, as all translations are multilingually aligned. It includes rich metadata supporting document-level translation, multimodal translation, and text classification tasks.
creator: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, Angela Fan (Facebook AI Research, LORIA)
inLanguage: 101 languages including English, Spanish, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, and 94 others
citeAs: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, Angela Fan. 2021. The FLORES-101 Evaluation Benchmark for Low-Resource and Multilingual Machine Translation. arXiv:2106.03193v1 [cs.CL]
rai:dataCollection: All source sentences were extracted from English Wikipedia, covering three domains: Wikinews (international news articles), Wikijunior (age-appropriate nonfiction books for children), and WikiVoyage (travel guides). Sentences were manually selected by 10 annotators from the research lab, who selected 3-5 contiguous sentences from randomly chosen articles. The selection process balanced paragraph locations (beginning, middle, end) across the corpus. For each sentence, metadata including Wikipedia URL, topic, boolean flags for linked entities and images were extracted.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: English Wikipedia articles from three sources: Wikinews (collection of international news articles), Wikijunior (age-appropriate nonfiction books for children from birth to age 12), and WikiVoyage (travel guide with articles about travel tips, food and destinations around the globe). One third of sentences were collected from each source.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The sentence selection process consisted of selecting an article at random from each source (Wikinews, Wikijunior, WikiVoyage), then manually selecting 3-5 contiguous sentences from each article, avoiding segments with very short or malformed sentences. Paragraph locations were balanced to be equally distributed across the whole corpus (one third from beginning, one third from middle, one third from end of articles). All sentences were manually labeled by sub-topic (one of 10 possibilities: crime, disasters, entertainment, geography, health, nature, politics, science, sports, and travel).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Professional translators translated all 3001 English sentences into 101 languages through Language Service Providers (LSPs). The translation workflow included: (1) translation and editing by an initial LSP, (2) automatic quality control checks including language identification, copy detection from commercial translation engines, length verification, and fluency checks, (3) quality assurance by an independent LSP that provided a translation quality score (0-100 scale) based on identified errors (grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition/omission, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, register), with severity levels (minor, major, critical). If the translation quality score was below 90%, translations were sent back for re-translation. The process could repeat for multiple rounds until the 90% threshold was met. Two translation LSPs were selected based on pilot experiments evaluating translation quality across multiple providers.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Translation quality was assessed through a Translation Quality Score (0-100 scale) determined by the number and severity of identified errors. Error types examined included: grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition or omission of information, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, and register. Each error was associated with a severity level (minor, major, critical). The acceptable translation quality score threshold was set to 90% based on pilot experiments. Evaluators were instructed to pay particularly high attention to unnatural translation errors. The largest error category across all languages was mistranslation, which included incorrect interpretation of source text, literal translations, mistranslations of phrasal verbs, and lack of disambiguation of ambiguous terms.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 professional translation per sentence per target language
rai:annotatorDemographics: Professional translators were employed through Language Service Providers (LSPs). The sentence selection process was performed by 10 annotators in the research lab: 6 male and 4 female, with different roles (researchers including scientists and engineers, and program/project managers), originally from different regions (East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America, and North America).
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains sentences about various topics including crime, disasters, entertainment, geography, health, nature, politics, science, sports, and travel. The sentence selection annotators came from different geographic regions (East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America, North America) and had different roles and genders.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to foster progress in machine translation for low-resource languages. The majority of the world's population speak low-resource languages and would benefit from improvements in translation quality on their native languages. By publicly releasing a high-quality and high-coverage dataset, the authors hope to enable better assessment of model quality on the long tail of low-resource languages and support evaluation of many-to-many multilingual translation systems.
rai:dataBiases: All source sentences were extracted from English Wikipedia, which means that non-English translations are produced by human translators rather than being original native text. While translationese (overly literal or awkward translations) has known idiosyncrasies, the authors conjecture that these effects are marginal when evaluating models in low-resource languages where current MT systems produce many severe mistakes. The authors note that evaluating translationese is a caveat of the many-to-many evaluation approach, though they believe the benefits of supporting traditionally neglected regionally-relevant language pairs outweigh this risk.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset consists of translations from English source sentences rather than original text in each language, which introduces translationese effects. The evaluation is limited to sentence-level and document-level translation tasks. Several low-resource languages have very limited training data available (some with less than 100K sentences of parallel data through English and no monolingual data), making translation quality particularly challenging for these languages. The authors note that translation between all languages in a many-to-many fashion requires improvement, as evidenced by overall quite low average spBLEU scores. Some language families (Bantu, Dravidian, Indo-Aryan, and Nilotic) show particularly poor performance with average spBLEU below 5 points.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for evaluation of machine translation systems, particularly for low-resource and multilingual translation. It supports: (1) many-to-many multilingual translation evaluation (10,100 language pairs), (2) document-level translation evaluation (multiple contiguous sentences from same article with URLs provided), (3) multimodal translation evaluation (metadata includes boolean flags for images and hyperlinked entities), (4) other tasks such as sentence and document classification, language identification, and multilingual domain adaptation. The dataset includes three splits: dev (for hyper-parameter tuning), devtest (for testing during development phase), and test (available only through evaluation server to prevent overfitting).
